William Jennings Bryan. A dominant figure in American politics for three decades, a three-time presidential candidate and fiery orator who championed agrarian interests and anti-establishment reform. He rose to national prominence in eighteen ninety-six with his legendary Cross of Gold speech at the Democratic National Convention, which electrified rural voters opposed to monetary policies favoring Eastern industrialists. Though he never won the presidency, Bryan reshaped the Democratic Party and became the moral voice of American populism.

Born in Salem, Illinois, Bryan became a lawyer and Nebraska Congressman known for his moral oratory and anti-establishment rhetoric. He delivered the iconic Cross of Gold speech at the eighteen ninety-six Democratic Convention, declaring: You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns. You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold.

Bryan ran for president three times—eighteen ninety-six, nineteen hundred, and nineteen oh-eight—each time losing to Republican opponents despite commanding passionate support among farmers and laborers. He championed free silver, unlimited coinage of silver at a fixed ratio to gold, as a remedy for agricultural depression and rural debt. He criticized industrial monopolies and railroad trusts and was a leading voice of the populist and progressive movements attacking corporate power.

Later in life, Bryan served as Secretary of State under Woodrow Wilson from nineteen thirteen to nineteen fifteen, opposing American entry into World War I on pacifist grounds. He became a cultural symbol of rural and religious America. His passionate defense of Christian fundamentalism during the nineteen twenty-five Scopes trial was his final major public moment and legacy.
